text: Two retirees, same $1 million, the same $60 ,000 a year to live on. One of them can run out of money, the other never will. Here's the difference. Meet James. He puts all of it into the S &P 500 fund, boo, and takes out 6 % a year. That's $60 ,000, but here's the problem. James retires right into a rough market, down 15%, then down 10, then down 5. But his bills don't stop, so he needs to keep selling even at the bottom. In three years, his million is down to $575 ,000. Now, meet Carol, the same million, the same $60 ,000 a year, same bad start, but this time she buys income first. She puts $500 ,000 into a private pension account paying 6 .5%. That's $32 ,500 every year for the rest of her life, no matter what the market does. The other $500 ,000 goes into boo, and she only needs $27 ,500 a year from it. $32 ,500 plus $27 ,500 is the same $60 ,000 as James. So, same income, same bad start, but here's what happens. If the market averages 9 % after that, then we'll be fine. James actually ends up with more money on paper, about $859 ,000 after 20 years. Carol has about $606 ,000 plus her $32 ,000 coming in every year. But if the markets were to average a little less, about $6 .6, James runs out of money completely. In year 26, Carol, she still has money invested, and her $32 ,500 shows up every year for the rest of her life. James actually ends up with more on paper, about $859 ,000 after 20 years. Carol has $600 ,000 plus $32 ,500 still coming in. That's the sequence of returns risk. When you're living off of your money, a bad start can break your plan, even if the averages look fine. James is hoping that the market cooperates. Carol has a paycheck. If you're within 10 years of retirement or are already there, DM me the word INCOME, and I'll stress test your plan.
